analysis.one_liner: Gives many workers twelve weeks of unpaid, job-protected leave for a new child or serious illness.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed the leave guarantee 71-27 through its companion H.R. 1 after folding this bill into it, and it became the first law signed by President Clinton in 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would require employers with 50 or more workers to let eligible employees take up to 12 weeks of unpaid leave in a year to have or adopt a child, to recover from a serious health condition, or to care for a spouse, child, or parent with one, and to get their job or an equivalent one back afterward. Employers would have to keep paying the employee's health insurance during the leave. The leave is unpaid unless the worker has accrued paid time to swap in, and firms with fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles of a worksite are exempt.
analysis.who_benefits: Employees who have worked at least 12 months and 1,250 hours for an employer with 50 or more workers — roughly, most workers at midsize and large firms. They gain the right to take time off for a birth, adoption, foster placement, their own serious illness, or a family member's serious illness without losing their job or health coverage. Federal civil servants and congressional employees get the same protections under separate titles of the bill.

how_it_helps.text: Entitles eligible employees to 12 workweeks of unpaid leave per 12-month period for the birth or adoption of a child, care for a spouse, child, or parent with a serious health condition, or their own serious health condition.
Requires the employer to restore the worker to the same job or an equivalent position with equivalent pay and benefits on return, without loss of benefits accrued before the leave.
Requires employers to maintain group health coverage during the leave at the same level as if the worker had kept working.
Makes it unlawful for an employer to interfere with or discriminate against a worker for exercising these rights, with damages, reinstatement, and attorney's fees available in court.
Extends the same leave rights to federal civil service employees and, under a separate title, to Senate and House employees.

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 50 or more employees, who must hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, continue paying health premiums for workers on leave, and often pay for temporary replacements — with no offsetting federal subsidy. The cost is blunted because the leave is unpaid and because firms under the 50-employee threshold are exempt.

drawbacks.text: The leave is unpaid: the bill only lets workers substitute accrued paid vacation, sick, or personal leave if they have it, so the lowest-wage workers — those with the least savings — often cannot afford to use the benefit.

Coverage is narrow: workers at worksites where the employer has fewer than 50 employees within 75 miles are excluded, as are workers with less than 12 months or 1,250 hours of service, leaving out many part-time and new workers.

Employers bear real costs with no compensation — maintaining health premiums during leave, covering absence with temps or overtime — which supporters of a stronger bill acknowledged by adding employer-side protections like notice rules, medical certification, employer-paid second opinions, and the right to deny reinstatement to the highest-paid 10 percent of a facility's workforce to prevent grievous economic injury.
Spouses who work for the same employer can have their combined leave capped at 12 weeks for a birth, adoption, or care of a sick parent, rather than each getting 12 weeks.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The gain for workers is real but modest: job security during life's biggest disruptions, without any pay. The cost to employers is limited by the unpaid design, the small-business exemption, and built-in employer safeguards, which is why the bill drew support from some Republicans and business-adjacent senators alongside labor's full backing. The honest criticism is that an unpaid mandate helps comfortable workers most and does least for the low-wage workers who need it most; a paid-leave program would have helped them more at far greater public cost.

outcome.mechanism: Rather than passing this bill itself, the Senate folded it into the House-passed H.R. 1 and passed that instead 71-27, then postponed this bill indefinitely; the companion measure became the Family and Medical Leave Act of 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Dodd introduced the bill on January 21, 1993 with 46 cosponsors — 38 Democrats and 8 Republicans.

The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee ordered the bill reported favorably on January 26 and reported it without amendment the next day, with minority views filed, and it was placed on the legislative calendar as Calendar No. 3.
The Senate took the bill up by unanimous consent on February 2 and debated it February 3-4; a cloture motion — a vote to end debate and force a final vote — was presented on February 3.

On February 4 the Senate incorporated the measure into H.R. 1 as an amendment and passed H.R. 1 in lieu of this bill by 71-27, with Democrats voting 55-2 in favor and Republicans 16-25, and then indefinitely postponed this bill by voice vote.

The enacted law covers congressional employees and federal civil servants alongside private-sector workers, and a later version of the measure added a Sense of Congress directing the Defense Secretary to review the policy on gay service members and report by July 15, 1993.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers at midsize and large employers gained a federal right to job-protected leave. Employers came out better than in earlier versions, because the enacted leave is unpaid, small firms are exempt, and employer safeguards were written in; the measure cleared only after two vetoes by President George H.W. Bush in prior Congresses, which is widely reported.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers at midsize and large employers

for.name: Sen. Christopher Dodd
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 21, 1993 and lined up 46 cosponsors, 38 Democrats and 8 Republicans.

for.name: Sen. Edward Kennedy
for.role: Chair, Senate Labor and Human Resources
for.what_they_did: Reported the bill from committee without amendment on January 27 with written report 103-3 and got it placed on the legislative calendar.

for.name: Sen. George Mitchell
for.what_they_did: Brought the bill to the floor by unanimous consent on February 2 and managed its consideration and incorporation into H.R. 1.

for.name: President Bill Clinton
for.what_they_did: Signed the companion measure H.R. 1 in February 1993 as the first law of his presidency, fulfilling a campaign pledge after two earlier vetoes of the same leave guarantee.

against.name: 25 of 43 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage of H.R. 1 carrying the leave mandate, 25 to 16.

against.name: U.S. Chamber of Commerce and business associations
against.what_they_did: Lobbied against a federal leave mandate across the multi-year fight over the bill, arguing it imposed uncompensated costs on employers.

against.name: President George H.W. Bush
against.what_they_did: Vetoed earlier versions of the family and medical leave bill in 1990 and 1992, keeping the mandate from becoming law until after he left office.

sides.party_line_note: Democrats backed the final vote almost unanimously, 55-2, while Republicans split 16 for and 25 against, for an overall 71-27.

industries.note: The bill obliges them to hold jobs open for up to 12 weeks, keep paying health premiums during leave, and fund temporary replacements, with no public subsidy. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs directly against workers' interest in keeping a job through a birth or illness, though the unpaid design and 50-employee threshold sharply limited the cost they actually bore.
Firms covering leave with temporary hires shift some work to staffing agencies, a modest secondary beneficiary of the mandate.
